e-9948.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve Given the Derivatives With Respect To X and Y
e-9948.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/a0eb20697f72b1ec5f06cc1ebfa4ba364c1023c915950b64cfab2367964db928.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = 2^{\theta}$ (shown above) given that

$$
y'(\theta) = 2^{\theta}(\ln 2\sin\theta+ \cos\theta), \qquad
x'(\theta) = 2^{\theta}(\ln 2\cos\theta-\sin\theta) .
$$
e-9948.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{2}^{\theta }(\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{{2}^{\theta }(\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9949.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve at a Point Given Derivatives With Respect To X and Y
e-9949.problem:
Find the slope of the tangent line to the polar curve $r = 1-\cos\theta$ at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ given that

$$
y'(\theta) = \cos\theta  - \cos2\theta, \qquad
x'(\theta) = -\sin\theta + \sin2\theta.
$$
e-9949.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at $\theta=\dfrac\pi4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $2$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{2}+2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}+2}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

e-10034.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Constant Polar Curve
e-10034.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/c86e5a3dd066efc462635310ff80973f468d04bad9206f410a74941ccf39f2f3.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = 2$  (shown above) at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$
e-10034.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r = 2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /3} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-628.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve
e-628.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/19b420204caf7f2706b4d355b5538dc347b5377d2b9f99297dbf6accc3220f59.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = \theta,$ shown above.
e-628.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r=\theta,$ we get

$$
x = \theta\cos\theta, \qquad y=\theta\sin\theta.
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta)\mathbin{:}$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

Find dydx for the polar curve r=2(1−cos⁡θ) (shown above) given that y′(θ)=2(cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)),x′(θ)=−2(sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)).

a
cos⁡θ−2cos⁡(2θ)2sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)
b
cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)
c
−2cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−2sin⁡(2θ)
d
−cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)
e
−sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)
Submit

decision.explanation: Use dy/dx = y′(θ)/x′(θ). Dividing the given derivatives cancels the factor 2 and leaves a minus sign, giving −(cos θ − cos(2θ))/(sin θ − sin(2θ)), which is option d.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/7580d53db6063a859e46addc9635b958e96ad798508dccb0705701d5b36c12b6.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )$ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )).
$$
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find dydx for the polar curve r=2(1−cos⁡θ) (shown above) given that y′(θ)=2(cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)),x′(θ)=−2(sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)).

a
cos⁡θ−2cos⁡(2θ)2sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)
b
cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)
c
−2cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−2sin⁡(2θ)
d
−cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)
e
−sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ)cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ).

Therefore, dydx=2(cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ))−2(sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ))=−cos⁡θ−cos⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ−sin⁡(2θ).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/7580d53db6063a859e46addc9635b958e96ad798508dccb0705701d5b36c12b6.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )$ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )).
$$
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find dydx for the polar curve r=4cos⁡θ (shown above) given that y′(θ)=4cos⁡(2θ),x′(θ)=−4sin⁡(2θ).

a
−cot⁡(2θ)
b
2tan⁡(θ)
c
−tan⁡(2θ)
d
tan⁡(2θ)
e
cot⁡(θ)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ).

Therefore, dydx=4cos⁡(2θ)−4sin⁡(2θ)=−cot⁡(2θ).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms dy/dx = y′(θ)/x′(θ) = 4cos(2θ)/(−4sin(2θ)) = −cot(2θ). Thus option a is correct; the deliberately submitted option e is incorrect.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/ab95faf73fa837d232a67a773afdbf456f5798d0f05de23e6ce44b41cddb1881.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )} \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta }$ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).

after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find dydx for the polar curve r=eθ (shown above) given that y′(θ)=eθ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ),x′(θ)=eθ(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ).

a
1
b
sin⁡θ−cos⁡θcos⁡θ+sin⁡θ
c
sin⁡θ+2cos⁡θ2cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ
d
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θcos⁡θ−sin⁡θ
e
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡θ−cos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ).

Therefore, dydx=eθ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)eθ(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)=sin⁡θ+cos⁡θcos⁡θ−sin⁡θ.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve Given the Derivatives With Respect To X and Y
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/393199da94e9cb9b2a5944ba899e883a12911f66755f2b5407f512626358d944.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta }$ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).
$$
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{-10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{-10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find dydx for the polar curve r=θ (shown above) given that y′(θ)=sin⁡θ+θcos⁡θ,x′(θ)=cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ.

a
cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ
b
cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θsin⁡θ+θcos⁡θ
c
−(cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ)
d
sin⁡θ+θcos⁡θ
e
sin⁡θ+θcos⁡θcos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ
Submit

decision.explanation: Use dy/dx = y′(θ)/x′(θ). Substituting the given derivatives gives (sin θ + θ cos θ)/(cos θ − θ sin θ), which matches option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/80c86c945ba74dca1a26c4e3c7dcd585fe57303c99d34007885d7ff4d7cfef58.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=\theta $ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ). We have, y′(π4)=eπ/2(cos⁡π4+2sin⁡π4)=eπ/2(22+2⋅22)=322eπ/2, and x′(π4)=eπ/2(2cos⁡π4−sin⁡π4)=eπ/2(2⋅22−22)=22eπ/2,

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=2\theta $  at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

We have,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+2(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2+0 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}-2(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =0-\pi  \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{-\pi } \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =7\pi /4} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=4$  (shown above) at $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =7\pi /4} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To find dydx, we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ.

Using the fact that r=12, we get

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

x′(θ)=−12sin⁡θ,y′(θ)=12cos⁡θ.

Therefore,

content.problem: Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=12$ at $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=12,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=12\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{12\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =2\pi /3} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =-(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r=\frac{\theta }{2\pi },$ we get

$$
x=\frac{\theta }{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{\theta }{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{\theta }{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{(\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{\theta }{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{(\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{2\pi }[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}{\frac{1}{2\pi }[\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]} \\  & =\frac{\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ).$

content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,$ we get

$$
x=(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={((\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={((\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, differentiation gives x′ = (e^θ/π)(cos θ − sin θ) and y′ = (e^θ/π)(sin θ + cos θ). Their ratio cancels e^θ/π and matches option d.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/dfc16cf0da1332a921899dc1d3ebcdf75a59de3d1323c83f81a61c665b135ea8.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi },$ shown above.
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi },$ we get

$$
x=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Find dydx for the polar curve r=eθπ, shown above.

a
cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ
b
cos⁡θ−sin⁡θcos⁡θ+sin⁡θ
c
cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ
d
cos⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡θ−sin⁡θ
e
−(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find dydx, we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ

Using the fact that r=eθπ, we get

x=eθπcos⁡θ,y=eθπsin⁡θ.

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi },$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi },$ we get

$$
x=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Find dydx for the polar curve r=e−3θ, shown above.

a
e−3θ(3sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
b
e−3θ(cos⁡θ−3sin⁡θ)
c
e−3θ(sin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ)
d
3sin⁡θ−cos⁡θsin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ
e
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡θ−cos⁡θ
Submit

decision.explanation: With x = e^(−3θ)cos θ and y = e^(−3θ)sin θ, x′ = e^(−3θ)(−3cos θ − sin θ) and y′ = e^(−3θ)(cos θ − 3sin θ). Dividing y′ by x′ and canceling the exponential gives (3sin θ − cos θ)/(sin θ + 3cos θ), option d.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/ed90c6464c78010f38c764a677bddd3c7da22920fe4db62769e02d05934c9d24.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r={e}^{-3\theta },$ shown above.
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r={e}^{-3\theta },$ we get

$$
x={e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y={e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={({e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={({e}^{-3\theta })}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{e}^{-3\theta }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={({e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={({e}^{-3\theta })}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-3\theta }(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-3\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{-{e}^{-3\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20
?

Find dydx for the polar curve r=e−3θ, shown above.

a
e−3θ(3sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
b
e−3θ(cos⁡θ−3sin⁡θ)
c
e−3θ(sin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ)
d
3sin⁡θ−cos⁡θsin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ
e
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡θ−cos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find dydx, we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ

Using the fact that r=e−3θ, we get

x=e−3θcos⁡θ,y=e−3θsin⁡θ.

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate x′(θ) and y′(θ):

  • First, we compute the derivative of x with respect to θ using the product rule: x′(θ)=(e−3θcos⁡θ)′=(e−3θ)′⋅cos⁡θ+e−3θ⋅(cos⁡θ)′=−3e−3θ⋅cos⁡θ+e−3θ⋅(−sin⁡θ)=−3e−3θcos⁡θ−e−3θsin⁡θ=−e−3θ(3cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)

  • Then, we compute the derivative of y with respect to θ using the product rule: y′(θ)=(e−3θsin⁡θ)′=(e−3θ)′⋅sin⁡θ+e−3θ⋅(sin⁡θ)′=−3e−3θ⋅sin⁡θ+e−3θ⋅(cos⁡θ)=−3e−3θsin⁡θ+e−3θcos⁡θ=e−3θ(−3sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)

Therefore,

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)=e−3θ(cos⁡θ−3sin⁡θ)−e−3θ(sin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ)=3sin⁡θ−cos⁡θsin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/ed90c6464c78010f38c764a677bddd3c7da22920fe4db62769e02d05934c9d24.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r={e}^{-3\theta },$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r={e}^{-3\theta },$ we get

$$
x={e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y={e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={({e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={({e}^{-3\theta })}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{e}^{-3\theta }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={({e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={({e}^{-3\theta })}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-3\theta }(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-3\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{-{e}^{-3\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$
